notes.1a: Most candidates gave an acceptable explanation although very few gained full marks.
notes.1b: The manufacturing account was generally well prepared with a number of fully correct accounts. Common errors included not correctly adjusting the prime cost figure and the incorrect inclusion within the statement of distribution costs.
notes.1c: The income statement was also well prepared with most candidates presenting the statement in the correct format without or with few errors. The most common errors were not adding back the factory profit and the omission or incorrect treatment of the decrease in provision for unrealised profit.
notes.1d: Most candidates did provide a decision but their justification was generally weak. Although the question specifically asked for ‘relevant calculations’ some candidates did not offer any calculations.
notes.2a: Few candidates were able to state more than one use of the notes with many just producing three examples of items within the financial statements.
notes.2b: This was well answered with some fully correct statements and nearly all candidates scored high marks. Despite being told that the reserves were maintained in their most flexible form some candidates did incorrectly use the revenue reserves before the capital reserves when accounting for the bonus issue. A limited number of candidates were unable to calculate the profit for the year correctly.
notes.2c: Most candidates scored reasonable marks by providing a decision with acceptable justification supported by calculations. There was ample scope to gain marks and most did mention the factor of the interest and repayment of the loan as well as other relevant points.
notes.3a: This was well answered with most candidates able to explain the role of an external auditor satisfactorily.
notes.3b: The explanations for note 2 were much better than those for note 1. Few candidates recognised that the training programme should be treated as an expense. The application of the accruals concept was invariably incorrect where it was identified. The treatment of the inventory was generally correct with many candidates accounting correctly for the obsolete goods. �PAGE�23
notes.3c: Most candidates were able to correctly process the inventory adjustment and correctly add back the amortisation but relatively few were able to deal with the training expenses and licence fee.
notes.3d: Some candidates stated that the software licence should be included at the unadjusted $60000 with few correctly stating $50000. There were many correct inventory valuations. Candidates often gained the retained earnings mark by correctly adding $215000 to their own revised profit figure. Relatively few candidates were awarded the other payables mark.
notes.3e: Most candidates gave a decision and provided a reasonable justification.
notes.4a: Some candidates produced two acceptable differences but many gave differences between the accounts of the organisations.
notes.4b: The income and expenditure account was well prepared with many candidates gaining full marks. The most common errors were the incorrect treatment of the coach trips and the omission of the irrecoverable debts.
notes.4c: The statement of financial position was also well prepared with a limited number of fully correct statements. Marks were often lost due to the incorrect processing of the bank balance.
notes.4d: Candidates were generally awarded two or three of the available marks. Most provided advice but many suggested an increase of the price without considering its effect on the already low demand.
notes.5a: Although few candidates were able to state sufficient advantages and disadvantages to gain full marks most demonstrated their knowledge of the key facts in this area.
notes.5b: The production budget was well prepared with many fully correct answers. A limited few treated the opening and closing inventories incorrectly and some also did not account for the maximum inventory holding.
notes.5c: Most candidates who had prepared the production budget correctly were able to then prepare the purchases budget correctly and some of those who had made errors with the production budget were able to bring their results forward and obtain full credit for the purchases budget.
notes.5d: This was well answered with most candidates correctly calculating the increased holding cost.
notes.5e: Few candidates answered the question asked and discussed the advantages and disadvantages to the business rather than the directors. Nearly all, however, did correctly highlight the risk of not being repaid.
notes.6a: Most candidates were able to calculate the required costs correctly. A limited few did not allocate the fixed costs and merely dealt with direct materials and labour.
notes.6b: Nearly all calculated the selling price correctly.
notes.6c: This was well answered with most being able to correctly state two disadvantages.
notes.6d: This was also well answered with many fully correct answers and no common errors.
notes.6e: Nearly all candidates were able to calculate the cost per unit and selling price. Those who had made errors in part (d) also invariably performed these calculations correctly using their own figures.
notes.6f: Responses were generally not satisfactory with few being able to explain the reasons for the change. �PAGE�24
notes.6g: There were relatively few correct calculations of the new profit and the reasons given for the change were often generic rather than considering the suggestion in relation to Alpha and Omega.
notes.general_comments:
Overall candidates performed reasonably well on the paper. It is important that candidates should show
workings to support their answers as otherwise they cannot get any credit for partially correct answers.
